hints: Look at what is added across the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in reaction 1 to make ethanol, and recall which type of attacking species an alkene attracts.
Remember the industrial way to add water to ethene, think about what form of water is used and which catalyst helps it add.
In reaction 2 ethanol becomes ethanal, decide if this is oxidation and what orange oxidising agent is used for alcohols.
To stop oxidation at the aldehyde stage, think about whether you heat under reflux or gently warm and remove the volatile product as it forms.
In reaction 6 chloroethane becomes ethylamine, identify what bond breaks and what nucleophile replaces chlorine.
Recall the exact form of ammonia and the sealed vessel condition needed to make a primary amine from a chloroalkane.
walkthrough:
Sort out reaction 1 from alkene to alcohol**
Picture ethene, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$. It has an electron rich $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond, so it attracts electrophiles, species that love electrons. Adding $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ across the double bond to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is therefore electrophilic addition.

Recall the hydration reagents**
You do not just mix ethene with cold water. In industry you pass steam, $\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$, over the alkene with concentrated phosphoric acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, as catalyst. That gives the $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ needed for ethanol.

Sort out reaction 2 from alcohol to aldehyde**
Ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, to ethanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$, is a partial oxidation, loss of hydrogen. The standard AS oxidant is acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 / \text{H}^+$.

Choose conditions to stop at ethanal**
Ethanal boils at a low temperature and is easily oxidised further to ethanoic acid. So you warm gently and distil off ethanal as soon as it forms. Never reflux here, because reflux would keep it in contact with oxidant and push it to the carboxylic acid.

Sort out reaction 6 from chloroalkane to amine**
Chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, to ethylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, replaces $\text{Cl}$ by $\text{NH}_2$. The $\text{NH}_3$ molecule uses its lone pair to attack the $\delta+$ carbon, kicking out $\text{Cl}^-$. That is nucleophilic substitution.

Recall the amination reagents**
Use excess alcoholic ammonia, not aqueous, to favour the amine product. Heat in a sealed tube or heat under pressure so the volatile $\text{NH}_3$ stays in contact with the halogenoalkane.

Final answer: Reaction 1: electrophilic addition; steam with concentrated phosphoric acid catalyst.
Reaction 2: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), warm and distil (do not reflux).
Reaction 6: nucleophilic substitution; alcoholic ammonia, heat in a sealed tube / heat under pressure.

hints: Start with the polarity of $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in ethanal and decide which atom the $\text{CN}^-$ nucleophile will attack.
Think where the pair of electrons from the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ pi bond must go when the new $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond forms.
Consider how the negatively charged oxygen intermediate removes $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCN}$ and what bond in $\text{HCN}$ supplies that pair to regenerate $\text{CN}^-$.
walkthrough:
See why cyanide attacks carbon**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbonyl is polarised as $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$. The carbon is electron poor. The cyanide ion, $:\text{CN}^-$, has a lone pair on carbon and acts as a nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow from that lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$.

Move the double bond onto oxygen**
As the new $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond forms, the pi electrons of $\text{C}=\text{O}$ cannot stay on carbon. Draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ double bond to, or just beyond, the O atom. This gives the alkoxide intermediate $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CN})\text{O}^-$.

Use HCN to protonate and regenerate catalyst**
The $\text{O}^-$ is strongly basic. It takes $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCN}$. Show a curly arrow from the lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ to the $\text{H}$ of $\text{H}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, and a curly arrow from the $\text{H}-\text{C}$ bond back onto the $\text{C}$ to reform $:\text{CN}^-$. The products are $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ plus regenerated $\text{CN}^-$.

Final answer: Nucleophilic addition: $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ shown on ethanal.
Curly arrow from lone pair on $:\text{CN}^-$ to $\text{C}$ of $\text{C}=\text{O}$, and curly arrow from $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond to O.
Curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ intermediate to $\text{H}$ of $\text{HCN}$, and curly arrow from $\text{H}-\text{C}$ bond to $\text{C}$ to reform $\text{CN}^-$.

hints: Look at the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group added in reaction 3 and recall its functional group name.
Look at the $\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ carbon in the product and count how many other carbons it is joined to in order to classify the alcohol.
walkthrough:
Name both groups in the cyanohydrin**
The product $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ contains $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, which is the nitrile group. It also contains $\text{C}-\text{OH}$ on a carbon attached to two other carbons ($\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CN}$), so that is a secondary alcohol group.

hints: Recall what hot dilute acid does to a nitrile group and what functional group $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ becomes.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid**
Heating with dilute acid adds two molecules of water across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. The $\text{CN}$ carbon becomes a carboxylic acid carbon. So $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ becomes $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{COOH}$, which is 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, commonly called lactic acid. The alcohol group is unchanged.
